THE FOX AND THE LITTLE HEN

Once there was a little red hen who lived in a small house at the edge
of the wood. She kept her house clean and bright, and every morning
she swept the floor and fed her chicks. She was a busy hen, and a
careful one, for she knew that the sly old fox lived in the wood.

The fox was hungry all the time. Every day he sat under the trees and
looked at the little house. "One day I will catch that hen," he said
to himself, "and I will take her home for my dinner." But the little
hen always kept her door shut, and she never went far from home.

One day the fox had a plan. He put on an old coat and a big hat, and
he went to the door of the little house. He knocked three times. "Who
is there?" called the hen. "I am a poor old man," said the fox in a
soft voice. "I am cold and tired. Please open the door and let me sit
by your fire."

The little hen looked out of the window. She saw the big hat and the
old coat, but she also saw a long red tail under the coat. "I am
sorry," she said, "but my fire is very small, and my chicks are
sleeping. Go to the farm down the road. The farmer is kind, and his
fire is big." The fox did not want to go to the farm, for the farmer
had two big dogs.

The next day the fox came back again. This time he had a basket of
sweet berries. "Little hen," he called, "I have brought you a present.
Open the door and you can have all of these berries." The hen was very
fond of berries, but she was wiser still. "Thank you," she said,
"please leave the basket by the door. I will get it when you are
gone." The fox was angry, and he ran back into the wood with his
basket.

On the third day the fox did not knock at all. He hid behind the wood
pile and waited for the hen to come out. But the little hen had seen
him from her window. She called to her friend the goose, who lived by
the pond. The goose came running, flapping her great white wings and
making a terrible noise. The fox was so frightened that he ran away,
and he never came back to the little house again.

After that the little red hen and her chicks lived in peace. They
worked in the garden, they played in the sun, and in the evening they
sat by their small fire. And when the chicks asked for a story, the
hen always told them about the sly old fox and the brave white goose.

THE END

THE ANT AND THE DOVE

An ant went to the bank of a river to drink. The water was moving
fast, and the ant fell in and was carried away. A dove sat in a tree
that hung over the water. She saw the ant and dropped a leaf into the
river. The ant climbed onto the leaf and floated safely to the bank.

Not long after, a man came into the wood with a net to catch birds. He
saw the dove in the tree and he crept close, ready to throw his net.
The ant saw what he was going to do. She ran up to the man and bit him
on the foot. The man cried out and dropped his net, and the dove flew
away to safety.

One good turn deserves another.

THE BOY AND THE NUTS

A boy put his hand into a jar of nuts. He took as many as his hand
could hold. But when he tried to pull his hand out, the neck of the
jar was too small. He did not want to let go of any nuts, so he began
to cry. His mother said, "Take only half as many, and your hand will
come out." Do not try to do too much at once.

WHAT THE ANIMALS SAID

Little Ned went out to the farm one fine morning to say good day to
all the animals.

"Good day, Cow," said Ned. "What do you do all day?" "I eat the green
grass and give you milk," said the cow.

"Good day, Sheep," said Ned. "What do you do all day?" "I grow my soft
wool, so you can have a warm coat," said the sheep.

"Good day, Hen," said Ned. "What do you do all day?" "I lay eggs for
your breakfast," said the hen.

Then Ned sat down on the grass and thought. "Everyone has a job but
me," he said. The old dog came and put his head on Ned's knee. "Your
job is to be kind to all of us," said the dog. So Ned went home and
was kind all day.

The cow says moo,
The sheep says baa,
The hen says cluck,
And Ned says ha!

LITTLE SONGS FOR LITTLE PEOPLE

The rain is falling on the hill, the wind is blowing high, the little
birds are in their nests until the storm goes by. Then out they come
to sing and play, and fly up to the sky, and thank the sun for one
more day, and so, good day, say I.

The moon is up, the stars are out, the lamb is in the fold. Come in,
come in, my little one, the night is getting cold. Your bed is warm,
your cup is full, your mother is near by. So close your eyes and go to
sleep, and dream until the morning comes.

AN INQUIRY INTO THE PRINCIPLES OF TRADE

The division of labour, by which the produce of industry is greatly
augmented, arises not from any original wisdom of the legislature, but
from a certain propensity in human nature to truck, barter and
exchange one thing for another. This propensity is common to all men,
and to be found in no other race of animals.
